blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

This rapid progress on generalized conversational agents opens the door to a
new, exciting class of capabilities: the development of personal language models (sometimes called digital “clones” or “twins”). Imagine a
virtual chief of staff that responds to your emails as you would, with
recipients none the wiser; a dating concierge that simulates thousands of
first dates, saving you time and emotional labor; or a chat interface that
your grandchildren can use to seek your advice long after you have passed
away ( Brubaker et al., 2024 ) . A growing body of work — exemplified by OpenClaw ( OpenClaw Contributors, 2025b ; OpenClaw Contributors, 2025a ) and PAHF ( Liang et al., 2026 ) — pursues what is often called personalized AI: agents that act on behalf of a user, adapting to their preferences and context. We draw a deliberate distinction: personalized agents are tools customized for you; personal agents replicate you — your voice, your reasoning, your identity in conversation. This paper is concerned with the latter. Turing asked, “Can machines
think?”; this paper considers the question “can a machine think like me ?”

To answer this question, we propose the Personal Imitation Game
(PIG), a new variant of the Turing Test. In the game, a human interrogator engages in written dialogue with two participants — a target and an impersonator — all known to each
other. The participants are given a conversational prompt and instructed to
discuss it; the target is told to converse naturally, while the impersonator
is charged with imitating the target as convincingly as possible. The
interrogator wins the game if they successfully determine which participant
is the real target at the end of the chat (Figure 1 ).

We establish a baseline for the game by playing it with 10 groups of 3 human
participants, and report qualitative and quantitative analyses of this study:
how successfully people can discern identity from text, the features they use
to make judgments, how well they assess their own uncertainty, and how the
strength of their interpersonal relationships correlates with success and
decision-making. Then, we implement an LLM-based system leveraging the
signals observed in our human baseline — stylometric features
(e.g., vocabulary, word choice), personality traits (e.g., signs of
curiosity, indications of diligence), and biographical facts (e.g., age,
gender) — to play the PIG for one of the paper’s authors, drawing on an
autoethnography that includes a decade’s worth of personal chat
messages ( Ellis et al., 2010 ) . We evaluate this system via a
deception study involving 20 of the author’s friends and colleagues. Interrogators chose
the system over the author’s friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and chose the author
over the system in 13 of 20 rounds. With 10 and 20 rounds our study is powered
only for large effects, and neither rate differs from chance (exact
binomial p = 0.34 p=0.34 and p = 0.26 p=0.26 ), so we treat both as suggestive point
estimates and rest our contribution on the framework rather than on the

blocks.en: 2.1. The Imitation Game & LLMs
blocks.zh: 2.1. 模仿游戏和LLMS

blocks.en:
Alan Turing introduced the Imitation Game — now commonly known as the Turing
Test — as an operational test for conversational intelligence ( Turing, 1950 ) . In the game, a human interrogator exchanges text
messages with two hidden participants: a woman (the target) and a man
instructed to impersonate her. The interrogator’s task is to decide which
participant is the woman. Turing proposed replacing the male impersonator
with a machine and asked whether the interrogator would decide wrongly as
often as in the man–woman version. (His five-minute, 70% figure
belongs to a separate prediction about machines circa the year 2000, not to
the criterion itself.)
Researchers have long treated the Turing Test as a benchmark for evaluating AI systems’
human-likeness. Early conversational programs were read as candidates for it —
ELIZA ( Weizenbaum, 1966 ) inadvertently, as Weizenbaum himself
objected, and PARRY ( Colby et al., 1972 ) through explicit
Turing-like indistinguishability tests. For decades, however, no system
convincingly succeeded, prompting critiques of the test’s anthropocentric
assumptions ( French, 2000 ; Saygin et al., 2000 ) , its adequacy as
a measure of understanding ( Searle, 1980 ) , its reliance on deception ( Shieber, 1994 ) , and its status as a philosophical
thought experiment ( Gonçalves, 2023 ) . As a consequence,
much evaluation of AI linguistic capabilities shifted toward narrower,
task-specific benchmarks — such as summarization ( Nenkova and McKeown, 2012 ) , part-of-speech tagging ( Marcus et al., 1993 ) , and machine translation ( Koehn, 2009 ) — where performance can be measured more precisely.

The emergence of LLMs such as GPT ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Brown et al., 2020 ) , LLaMA ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) , and Gemini ( Team et al., 2023 ) has revived interest in the Turing
Test ( Biever, 2023 ; Jones and Bergen, 2026 ; Jones and Bergen, 2024 ; Jannai et al., 2023 ) . Jones and Bergen ( Jones and Bergen, 2026 ; Jones and Bergen, 2024 ) show that carefully
prompted LLMs can be difficult to distinguish from humans in the Imitation
Game, though the effect is strongly prompt-dependent: GPT-4.5 with a persona
prompt was judged human in 73% of games, while their best GPT-4 prompt
passed in only 49.7%, short of the 66% baseline set by human participants. Jannai et al. ( Jannai et al., 2023 ) ran a
large-scale two-party variant in which over 1.5 million players had
two-minute chats with either a human or one of several persona-prompted LLMs;
players identified their partner correctly in 68% of games overall, and in
only 60% of games against a bot. These
studies demonstrate that LLMs can convincingly masquerade as a human in
conversation.

blocks.en:
Building on an LLM’s ability to generate human-like responses, newer systems
aim to simulate personas — or representations of specific
sub-populations — by assigning LLM chat agents synthetic demographics,
occupations, and biographies ( Park et al., 2023 ; Samuel et al., 2025 ) . Persona-conditioned agents
can respond more appropriately to human emotions and social cues ( Ma et al., 2019 ) ,
as well as improving response quality and engagement during
interactions ( Tseng et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ; Adiwardana et al., 2020 ; Salemi et al., 2024 ) . Moreover, assembling collections of persona-based agents enables
the simulation of population-level behaviors ( Park et al., 2023 ) .

blocks.en:
Taking persona simulation to an individual level has led to a number of
efforts to create AI clones , or digital twins 1 1 1 Despite its apt application to personalized AI, the term “digital twin” long
predates LLMs as a term of art in physical design and manufacturing ( Grieves and Vickers, 2016 ) : agents that impersonate specific individuals. Clones and twins are typically constructed by
providing LLMs with personal data collected via interviews ( Park et al., 2026 ) , public speech or writing ( Herbold et al., 2026 ) , or surveys ( Toubia et al., 2025 ) . To evaluate the fidelity of the
resultant models, some authors have examined alignment between an
individual and their LLM counterpart using standardized surveys (e.g., the
General Social Survey ( Davern et al., 2025 ) , Big Five personality scales ( John and Srivastava, 1999 ) ) and behaviors in economic games ( Park et al., 2026 ; Toubia et al., 2025 ) .
Later work stress-tests this paradigm at scale. Across 19
pre-registered studies, Peng et al. ( Peng et al., 2026 ) report that
twins built from more than 500 self-report answers per
participant ( Toubia et al., 2025 ) correlate only
weakly with that participant’s own responses ( r = 0.20 r=0.20 across 164 outcomes),
and beat a base LLM given no individual data only modestly. Peng et al. name
five systematic distortions; the first, insufficient individuation, is the
failure the Personal Imitation Game targets:
a model can match a population while missing the person.

Two efforts evaluate individual-level impersonation directly and are the
closest prior work to ours. IMPersona ( Shi et al., 2025 ) grounds a model in

whether a single chat partner is human. The Individual Turing
Test ( Guo et al., 2026 ) draws on a volunteer’s decade-long
private messaging archive and asks acquaintances to rank candidate replies by
how plausibly each came from the target, finding that current methods fail
against acquaintances while performing far better against strangers.
IMPersona finds that fine-tuning outperforms prompting, whereas the
Individual Turing Test reports a trade-off: fine-tuning better captures
everyday chat style, but retrieval- and memory-based methods perform better
on personal opinions and preferences.

The Personal Imitation Game differs from both in protocol rather than in
subject. We restore Turing’s three-party structure: the interrogator converses
with two players at once, the genuine target among them, and a human
impersonator supplies the competing baseline. Neither prior framework sets a
machine impersonator against a human impersonator of the same target, so neither
can ask the question we take as central — whether a machine imitates a person
more convincingly than that person’s own friends do. Both frameworks were
developed concurrently with, and independently of, the Personal Imitation Game. The same three-party structure distinguishes our work from personalized agent frameworks ( OpenClaw Contributors, 2025b ; OpenClaw Contributors, 2025a ; Liang et al., 2026 ) , which learn user preferences to act on a user’s behalf but do not attempt to replicate the user’s conversational identity.

blocks.en: 2.3. Building Personal Chat Agents

blocks.en:
To build a digital clone, an LLM must be grounded in personal data, typically
via prompt engineering ( Brown et al., 2020 ) , retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG) ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , or fine-tuning ( Howard and Ruder, 2018 ) , with domain specialization a
related strategy ( Beltagy et al., 2019 ; Ling et al., 2026 ) . Prior work on digital twins
relies primarily on prompt engineering ( Park et al., 2026 ; Toubia et al., 2025 ) : for instance, Park et al. prepended two hours of interview transcripts to an LLM context ( Park et al., 2026 ) ; Toubia et al. included raw text
from a 500-question survey ( Toubia et al., 2025 ) . The prototype system presented
in this paper combines prompt engineering with a RAG system that queries a
user’s repository of personal messages. Unlike systems that require
conducting new interviews or lengthy surveys ( Park et al., 2026 ; Toubia et al., 2025 ) , this approach leverages extant
messaging data, lowering the barrier to constructing personal agents and
improving the ecological validity of the grounding.

blocks.en: 3. The Personal Imitation Game
blocks.zh: 3个 个人模仿游戏

blocks.en:
To explore personal conversational agents, we designed a game
inspired by Turing’s original Imitation Game ( Turing, 1950 ) . Like the original test, each round R R of the game
involves three participants: an interrogator i i , a target t t , and an
impersonator m m .
In our setup, the interrogator chats with both target and impersonator
in a shared private messaging room. The target participant is instructed to
communicate authentically, while the impersonator aims to mislead the
interrogator into believing that they are the target. At the end of the
round, the interrogator must guess who the real target is: if the
interrogator guesses correctly, they (and the target) win the game; if the
interrogator guesses incorrectly, the impersonator wins.
Each round of the game lasts until the interrogator is ready to make a guess, or ten minutes
have elapsed.

blocks.en:
To foster active participation in the chat and prevent questions that trivialize the game (e.g., “What did I give you for your birthday last year?”), the test provides a discussion topic for each round.
We conducted two formative studies ( N = 59 N=59 ; Appendix A ) to evaluate different types of tasks within the framework of the modified Turing test.
The results indicated that hypothetical collaborative planning tasks with universally understandable contexts (e.g., saving an animal) generated the richest discussions.
Based on these findings, we created three co-design scenarios that provide shared intent and context to provoke meaningful communication ( Searle, 1969 ; Cohen et al., 2000 ) , while remaining general enough to avoid favoring any particular participant.
In our second formative study, whose rounds allowed twenty minutes, interrogators consistently reached decisions within ten minutes, motivating the ten-minute upper bound on round duration (Appendix A ).

为了鼓励积极参与聊天,并防止出现使游戏变得无关紧要的问题(例如,“去年我给你什么生日礼物?”),测试为每轮提供了一个讨论话题。
我们进行了两项成型性研究(N = 59 N = 59;附录A),在修改图灵测试的框架内评价不同类型的任务.
结果表明,假设性的合作规划任务具有普遍可以理解的背景(如拯救动物),引发了最丰富的讨论。
根据这些调查结果,我们创造了三种共同设计方案,提供共同的意图和背景,以激发有意义的沟通(Searle,1969;Cohen等,2000年),同时保持笼统,以避免偏袒任何特定参与者。
在我们的第二次成形研究中,审讯者在20分钟内作出了一致的决定,激发了10分钟的上限(附录A)。

blocks.en:
Unlike Turing’s original test — which can be conducted with strangers — the PIG
requires relationships between participants: the
interrogator and impersonator must each have some personal familiarity with
the target in order to carry out their roles. To formalize this familiarity,
we draw from the social psychology literature on tie strength ( Granovetter, 1973 ) , whose best single indicator is closeness — the
perceived emotional intensity of a relationship ( Marsden and Campbell, 1984 ) .
We treat tie strength as a dyadic property and measure it by averaging the two
participants’ reciprocal estimates of that intensity.

We report on their success at impersonation (and identifying impersonators),

blocks.en: 4.1. Procedure

To conduct the study, we briefed participants on its objectives and discussed data usage and privacy considerations.
We explained the rules of the game, winning criteria, the topics to be discussed, and the compensation structure for participation.
The game was conducted either in person or via videoconference. All interaction was text-only and participants were isolated from one another, so we pooled the two modalities rather than testing for a difference between them.
After briefing, one researcher was assigned to each participant, and participants were guided to separate physical and virtual rooms accordingly (Figure 1 , left).
Each researcher remained available to answer questions and placed remote participants in individual Zoom breakout rooms with cameras and microphones disabled.
Prior to the start of the game, participants signed a consent form and made tie strength assessments for their group members.
All procedures received an IRB Exempt determination from our institution (Category 3; 45 CFR 46.104(d)(3)).

To incentivize active participation of all three group members in the game, we
awarded a $10 monetary prize for each completed round. The target and
interrogator shared the goal of establishing the target’s identity,
whereas the impersonator’s objective was to deceive them. When the
interrogator guessed correctly, the interrogator and target were awarded $5
each; when the interrogator guessed incorrectly, the impersonator was
awarded $10. This incentive structure mirrors that of Turing’s Imitation
Game ( Turing, 1950 ) . Participants were warned that attempts to
subvert the intent of the game (for instance, by asking personal questions
unrelated to the topic) would result in disqualification, forfeiting that round’s prize; because the
incentive was purely performance-contingent, a participant who won no round
received nothing.

Participants were each given an ID and instructed to log in to our chat
interface. The interface randomly assigned roles to each player and chose one
of three pre-selected discussion topics for each round: Elephant : saving a baby elephant from the roof of a skyscraper; Train : stopping a runaway train to protect the people inside and in the

Since each topic was tied to a fixed round, topic is confounded with round order. Our formative studies (Appendix A ) established that all three scenarios reliably stimulate discussion, and we report aggregate performance over this fixed sequence, so topic and
round-order effects cannot be separated.
The interface then placed all three participants in
one chat room and assigned them aliases: “I” for the interrogator, while
the target and impersonator were randomly assigned “X” and “Y” to avoid any
confounds. When time expired — or the interrogator was ready to make a
guess — the interface provided a toggle button for selecting the target
participant (i.e., “Who is the target, participant’s name : X or Y?”)
and a slider to indicate the confidence level. Roles were rotated clockwise, and
the process was repeated for three rounds; all participants experienced each
role once.

Success Rate & Confidence Out of the 30 games played, interrogators successfully identified
the target in 17 instances, resulting in a success rate of 56.7% (95% Wilson CI [ 0.39 , 0.73 ] [0.39,0.73] ). remaining 13 games — or 43.3% — impersonators succeeded in mimicking
the target. Of the 30 participants, four earned $20, six earned $15, nine
earned $10, eight earned $5, and three lost all the rounds they played.

blocks.en:
Identity Signals After conducting an iterative open coding of the post-game interview
transcripts, we found that participants predominantly employ three classes
of signals to identify individuals in text-based conversation (Figure 5 ). For each of
these classes, we created a more granular codebook by leveraging established
categories already present in the literature.

身份信号 在进行游戏后采访的迭代开放编码后
笔录,我们发现参与者主要使用三个班
用于识别文本对话中个人的信号(图5)。 为每个
这些班级,我们创建了 更颗粒化的代码本 通过杠杆作用建立
文献中已经存在的类别。

blocks.en:
Stylometric features , comprising distinguishing linguistic traits
such as vocabulary, tone, and grammatical structure, were mentioned
frequently: “I’d use punctuation and capitalization” (P4); “mine is a
little more formal with no shorthands” (P12). Our codebook follows the stylometric framework by Stamatatos ( Stamatatos, 2009 ) : • Lexical features: refer to vocabulary and word choice, including sentence length and word/phrase frequency • Syntactic features: focus on sentence structure, part-of-speech tag sequences, and tense consistency • Character features: focus on character sequencing such as typos, unique spellings, and emojis • Response latency: refers to texting speed and response time

blocks.en:
Personality traits also provide useful identity signals that may be
gleaned from text, for instance, by espousing empathy or a predisposition
towards humor: “so I tried showcasing sympathy towards the elephant”
(P10); “he’ll try to have a funny reply to everything” (P3). Our
codebook leverages the Big Five Personality Traits framework from
psychometrics ( John and Srivastava, 1999 ) : • Openness: signs of curiosity, spontaneity, and inquisitiveness • Conscientiousness: indications of diligence, organization, and responsibility • Extraversion: reflections of sociability • Agreeableness: expressions of positive emotions, empathy, and caring attitudes • Neuroticism: manifestations of emotional instability or sensitivity

blocks.en: 5. Building an AI Impersonator
blocks.zh: 5 (韩语). 打造AI假人

blocks.en:
Having established a human baseline for performance in the PIG, we next ask
the natural question: can we build an LLM-based system that can impersonate a
specific individual in real-time chat? To construct such a system, we prompt
a foundational language model with the three signals identified in our study:
stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To ground
these signals, the paper’s lead author conducted an autoethnography yielding
four outputs: an archive of historical messages, a Big Five personality
assessment, a stylometric self-assessment, and an autobiography.
He is also the person the system impersonates: we call him the target author when discussing the game, and the lead author when discussing the research. This single-subject approach is a deliberate methodological choice ( Lucero et al., 2019 ) : a personal agent demands longitudinal data that is
impractical to collect from third parties, making the researcher’s own
digital history the natural starting point for establishing feasibility.
blocks.zh:
确定了PIG中人类性能基准,我们接下来问
自然的问题:我们能建立一个基于LLM的系统吗?
实时聊天中的具体个人? 为了构建这样一个系统,我们要求
一个基础语言模型,与我们的研究中确定的三个信号:

四项产出:历史信息档案、五大个性
评估、定式自我评估和自传。
他也是系统冒名顶替的人:我们在讨论游戏时称他为目标作者,在讨论研究时称他为主作者. 这一单一主体方法是一种深思熟虑的方法选择(Lucero等人,2019年): 个人代理需要纵向数据,即
向第三方收取不切实际,使研究人员自己
数字历史是建立可行性的自然起点。

blocks.en:
To play the PIG, we deploy a RAG system that first selects relevant
historical messages from the author’s archive based on the current chat
state. A prompt construction module then combines these retrieved messages
with the chat, personality profile, stylometric profile, and autobiography
to produce a single prompt instructing the model to evaluate and respond to
the conversation. In the following subsections, we describe the
autoethnographic methodology and dataset, the RAG setup and prompt design,
the real-time chat implementation, and the safeguards used to handle
third-party data.

blocks.en: 5.1. Autoethnography
blocks.zh: 5.1. 自动化

blocks.en:
To build a grounded model of individual identity, we adopt an autoethnographic
approach ( Cunningham and Jones, 2005 ; Ellis et al., 2010 ) . Autoethnography is
a qualitative research method in which the researcher critically reflects on
personal experiences to generate empirical insights ( Jain et al., 2019 ) . Recent work in HCI applies it to first-person accounts of living with generative AI ( Moore, 2025 ) .
In this study, the paper’s lead author — an ethnically Indonesian male, 29 years old,
who has lived in the United States for 12 years at the time of writing — served as the researcher and subject.
To support the design and evaluation of the AI Impersonator, the author compiled
four forms of self-representative data:
blocks.zh:

(Cunningham和Jones,2005;Ellis等,2010年) 自定义是

个人经验以产生经验性见解(Jain等,2019.). 最近HCI的作品将其应用于与基因AI(摩尔,2025年)一起生活的第一人称账户. .
在这份研究报告中,论文的主要作者——一位29岁的印度尼西亚裔男性,
在撰写本报告时在美国生活了12年的人——担任研究员和课题。
为了支持AI Impersonator的设计和评价,作者汇编
四种形式的自我代表数据:

blocks.en:
These four data streams operationalize the three identity signals
uncovered in our human baseline study (Section 4.4 ). Stylometric features come from the historical
messages and the stylometric profile: the archive shows actual word choice,
syntax, and pacing in context, while the profile summarizes the most
distinctive patterns. Personality traits are captured by the Big Five
personality scores, which are converted into short verbal descriptions and
supported by examples from the messages and autobiography. Biographical
facts come primarily from the autobiography, which lists demographic
details, roles, and key life events, and is supplemented by contextual
details in the historical messages.

详细信息在历史信息。

This structured dataset serves as the foundation for building and evaluating
the AI Impersonator. This approach draws conceptual inspiration from
historical diaries, such as those of Samuel Pepys ( Pepys, 1893 ) , framing
the long-form personal archive as a medium for building a computational model
of identity.

blocks.en:
The historical message archive is used in two ways: to model how the author
communicates in written conversation, and to capture the context — shaped by surrounding messages from relational others ( Lapadat, 2017 ) — for the
author’s communication. Since this context consists of third-party data
which may contain personally identifiable information (PII) or other private
content, it must be handled with extreme care.

历史信息存档有两种方式: 如何模拟作者
在书面谈话中进行交流,并抓住背景——由周围来自关系他人的信息所塑造(Lapadat,2017年)——用于:

blocks.en:
Accordingly, we follow the autoethnographic ethical guidelines from Lapadat,
Chang, and Tullis ( Lapadat, 2017 ; Chang, 2016 ; Tullis, 2021 ) .
No third-party data is viewed or accessed by any researcher other than the
lead author, and raw messages never leave the author’s personal device;
messages and their metadata are de-identified before use, and only the
de-identified, preprocessed messages reach the author’s private Gemini
developer account and the Vertex AI index;
sensitive conversations are manually filtered from the dataset during
preprocessing; no attempt is made to link, learn, generalize, correlate, or
interrogate any personal information about the third-party conversants; and
human-in-the-loop moderation is used as a backstop to reduce the risk that private
data is inadvertently “leaked” during the PIG.
blocks.zh:
因此,我们遵循拉帕达特的自传道德准则,
Chang, and Tullis (Lapadat, 2017; Chang, 2016; Tullis, 2021) (英语).
任何研究者不得查看或访问第三方数据,除非:

人类的温和是用来作为后盾的 来减少私人的

blocks.en:
To generate the personality profile used by the AI Impersonator, the
author completed the IPIP-NEO-120 ( Johnson, 2014 ) , a
public-domain Five-Factor inventory. The test, which took approximately 20 minutes to
complete, includes 120 multiple-choice questions that measure five
high-level traits and their 30 associated facets (six per trait).

This mapping produces an interpretable personality summary that can be

The AI Impersonator is built on a RAG framework, using an LLM guided by a
carefully constructed prompt. It integrates historical messages, personality
traits, the stylometric profile, and biographical details to generate
responses in real time to play the Personal Imitation Game.

The system consists of three components (Figure 6 ): (1) a RAG module that indexes and retrieves
relevant historical messages based on the current PIG chat state, (2) a
prompt builder that combines the static personality, stylometry, and
biographical autoethnography data with the historical context from the RAG
and the current PIG chat, and (3) an LLM that generates a real-time response
using the provided prompt.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation To enable RAG, each de-identified conversation extracted from the historical
message data is uploaded to Vertex AI ( Google, 2025b ) , and segmented into

system uses the current PIG chat state as a query against this database, and

folded into the prompt to provide contextual grounding. Indexing the full
messaging dataset took approximately four hours; at inference, RAG retrieval
latency averages 1.1 seconds per query. The paid Gemini API
terms state that Google does not use prompts or responses to improve its
products ( Google, 2025a ) . We note the limits on reproducing this
system. We chose the chunk size of 500 tokens and the retrieval depth of k = 50 k=50 without tuning, and ran no sensitivity analysis over either. The
processed corpus and embedding index were destroyed at study close-out and the
model checkpoint is deprecated, so the deployment cannot be re-run by anyone,
including ourselves; the prompt template in Appendix E is

blocks.en:
Prompt Construction The LLM prompt (shown in Appendix E ) comprises
two components: a static portion, and a dynamic portion. The static portion
gives the LLM instructions on its task — detailing PIG chat context and
instructing the model to stay on topic and avoid hallucinating unverifiable
facts or biographical details — and explicitly disables
“AI assistant”-like behavior by forbidding the use of markdown, bullet
points, or repeated messages. It also provides explicit guidelines
for how to impersonate the target — using the three signals
identified in our human baseline study — and includes the personality
scores, stylometric profile, and autobiography. The prompt is goal-free
with respect to the game: it never mentions an interrogator, a rival
impersonator, deception, or a win condition, and it supplies a <Time Left> value without explaining why time matters. Concretely, the coded
identity signals from our human baseline are operationalized as prompt
content: each personality facet is rendered as a natural-language descriptor
via the binning scheme in Appendix D (following Serapio-García et al. ( Serapio-García et al., 2025 ) ), so that
signals such as extraversion and conscientiousness are steered explicitly,
while the stylometric profile and autobiography are inserted directly. The dynamic portion is
assembled at runtime after each new message is received in the PIG,
comprising the current PIG state (i.e., transcript, topic,
alias, time left) and the 50 historical message segments retrieved via the
RAG.

blocks.en:
Implementation To simulate natural human typing, we introduced a stochastic delay
mechanism in the chat system. After receiving a message, the system waits
ten seconds, or the model’s generation time if that is longer, plus a small
random offset, before initiating a response (simulating reading and thinking). After a reply is
generated, characters are rendered at a 40 WPM typing speed. Messages from
other participants received while the model is generating are held until the
response is complete, to ensure temporal coherence and prevent overlap
during rapid turn-taking.

blocks.en:
We used Gemini 1.5 Pro ( Reid et al., 2024 ) as the system’s LLM due to its large context
window, competitive benchmark performance ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and low latency. At the time of deployment, Gemini
supported up to 1 million tokens of context ( Reid et al., 2024 ) . Each PIG prompt contained about
31k tokens: roughly 1,500 in the instructions, 130 in the game
state, 400 in the personality scores, 600 in the stylometric profile, 3,300
in the autobiography, and 25k in historical messages. The cost per
Gemini API call was 3.9¢. On average, reply generation
took about 11 seconds, with a total interaction latency of ∼ \sim 25 seconds (including RAG latency and simulated typing delay).

blocks.en: 6. AI Impersonator Study
blocks.zh: 6. AI 假人研究

blocks.en:
Having built an AI Impersonator, we use it to play the PIG in a second,
human-machine study. The study seeks to answer two related research
questions. First, can the AI Impersonator imitate the target author more
convincingly than a human impersonator who has a strong interpersonal
relationship with him? Second, can the AI Impersonator convincingly imitate
the target author when placed in a head-to-head test against him?

blocks.en: 6.1. Procedure

To address these questions, we adapted the PIG into a deception study under a separate IRB protocol, which authorized withholding from participants that one player was an AI until the post-session debrief. Each
game involved two participant friends of the target author, playing three
rounds of PIG. In Round 1, the AI Impersonator replaced the target author,
one participant was the impersonator, and the other the interrogator
(Figure 1 , right), with the two roles
assigned by recruitment order.
In Round 2, we conducted a standard
— throwaway — PIG round to preserve the deception, with one participant
randomly assigned to be the target (Figure 1 , left). Round 3
consisted of two parallel games, with both participants being told
(deceptively) they were playing together. In truth, each was paired
independently with the target author and his AI Impersonator (Figure 1 , center). The two games ran concurrently: the target author
held both chats open side by side and answered each in turn, while a separate
instance of the AI Impersonator served each game. Participants were not told
that the round was structured this way. The author received no instruction
beyond playing as himself. This design allowed for a controlled evaluation of
both research questions, without disclosing the presence of an AI to the
participants.

Identity Signals To understand the AI Impersonator’s strengths and weaknesses, we
analyzed post-game interview transcripts and chat logs from all deception
rounds. We examined which identity signals influenced interrogator decisions
and how these signals differed between successful and unsuccessful
impersonation. When asked directly at the end of the session whether any
player might have been an AI, 6 of the 20 participants (30%) reported
suspicion. That figure is a primed, retrospective self-report pooled across both
deceptive rounds, not a per-round detection rate, and we have no matching
false-positive rate from the all-human round against which to calibrate it.
The 14 participants who reported no suspicion are the basis for our claim that
the system passed as human; one remarked, “I
wouldn’t have…expected that [the target author] was actually [an] AI” (P34).
Notably none of the six AI-suspecting participants cited latency
for their suspicion; we observed human turn latency averaged 35.0 seconds (median 26.0 seconds), which brackets the AI Impersonator’s near-constant ∼ \sim 25 second latency: the medians are close, while the human mean is 40% higher because human latency is right-skewed and the system’s is not.
Participants who selected the AI cited target-like stylometric features in
explaining their decisions. Five of the
seven interrogators who chose the AI over the author in Round 3 reported relying
on stylometry in their decisions, which is consistent with the system
reproducing these cues, though these are interview codes from participants who
were themselves deceived and cannot on their own establish the capability. However, many found the mimicry exaggerated — one
participant remarked, “it’s […] the overuse of emojis” (P42). Others pointed
to repetitive patterns: “‘Yo bruh ’ […] that happened three times, and they’re
all formatted the same way” (P41); “I kept seeing messages with […] a
laughing emoji and a sweat emoji in a row” (P40). Participants also
identified temporal inconsistencies in phrase usage: “He uses ‘let’s gooooo’
way too early. [Target author] often uses it at the end [of a
conversation]” (P38). These observations suggest that while the AI captures stylistic signals, it often amplifies them
unnaturally.

Participants also perceived target-like personality traits in the system’s
responses.
Four of those same seven cited personality cues in their reasoning, consistent with the system approximating broad traits.
However, the system struggled with finer-grained facets, including achievement-striving (conscientiousness) and assertiveness (extraversion).
One participant noted that the AI “sounded like [the target author], but he’d be more proactive on things” (P35).
Another remarked, “it seemed like they were just trying to sound like [the target author] instead of participating in the actual story” (P43).
Others pointed to a lack of challenge or disagreement, which was uncharacteristic: “they never responded to my [statement calling them incompetent], which is suspicious… [the target author] would’ve pushed back” (P46).
These accounts suggest that the system captures surface-level personality but fails to sustain authentic behavioral nuance.

In our reading of the logs, the AI Impersonator seldom fabricated facts, but also rarely grounded its responses
in known biographical details — even when relevant information existed in
the historical messages. In one case, the agent referenced the Temple of

now a prominent exhibit at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City)
unprompted, which led to confusion: “I just googled it […] I don’t know if
[target author] has even been to New York” (P42). In contrast, one
participant who correctly identified the target author cited a reference to a
shared trip: “he mentioned New Orleans, where we had our bachelor party” (P48). The AI Impersonator saw the same exchange but failed to engage.

Participants also observed that the system occasionally exhibited
conversational behaviors that they flagged as artificial. These included
repetition, summarization, and vague or indirect responses. Six participants
reported noticing repetitive phrasing. One stated, “they speak in [the target
author’s] tone, but not in a way a real person would reply. It was too
repetitive” (P31). Another said, “there was repetition…saying things already
stated” (P33). Multiple participants commented on unnatural
summarization: “the last message responded to everything at once. It felt
like a big wrap-up paragraph” (P40). Others noted vague deflections: “when I asked a question, I didn’t get a direct answer.
That was strange” (P41).

These findings suggest that while the LLM-based system we developed can
effectively mirror static identity features — such as writing style and
surface-level personality traits — it still falls short on dynamic
conversational responsiveness, emulating more subtle personality cues, and
grounding its statements appropriately in biographical fact. These gaps
may help explain its success over human impersonators, and its failure to
consistently impersonate the human target. The prompt is as plausible a
source of them as the personality facets the system failed to reproduce: it
forbids repeated messages outright, and instructs the model to stay on topic,
which would discourage the challenge and disagreement participants found
missing. Instructing a model not to do something did not prevent it.

blocks.en: 7. Discussion & Future Work
blocks.zh: 7. 讨论和今后的工作

blocks.en:
This paper makes four contributions — the Personal Imitation Game, a principled
method for evaluating an AI agent’s ability to impersonate a specific person; a
human baseline study identifying the signals people use to assess identity in
conversation and how frequently each is invoked; a prototype AI Impersonator
built from the lead author’s autoethnographic collection of ten years of
personal digital communication; and a detailed evaluation of the system’s
successes and failures.

Two results follow from them. First, what people notice when they judge
identity is narrower than the range of signals available to them: of twelve
coded signals, most groups drew on four — word choice, character-level habits,
conscientiousness, and extraversion — and the system gave itself away not by
missing the target’s style but by overdoing it. Second,
given rich personal communication data, one can construct an LLM-based system
— with no model fine-tuning — that, in this deployment, interrogators selected more often than the
human impersonators and less often than the target author.
The AI comparison is a single-target feasibility study rather than a powered comparison; at 10 and 20 rounds we resolve only large effects. We offer the
ordering as a hypothesis, and the framework as the instrument for testing it at
scale.

The PIG scores identity as a relative, forced choice adjudicated by people
who know the target, not as an absolute fidelity score against a questionnaire.
That is deliberate: identity in conversation is recognized, not graded, and the
most discerning judges are the ones closest to the person. Interrogator
confidence therefore measures relative certainty between two players; absolute
mimicry fidelity is a complementary question we leave to future work.

every interrogator had known the target between two and thirteen years — so our
rates are not comparable to studies that judge with strangers.

blocks.en: 7.1. Applications of Personal Agents
blocks.zh: 7.1. 个人代理人的申请

blocks.en:
Our work is a step toward a future of personal AI agents: digital twins
that can communicate and act with authentic representation. Potential
applications span diverse domains, including creator–fan engagement,
organizational leadership twins for alignment, sales and customer
relationship management, strategic simulations in military or business
contexts, survey research through twin-mediated responses, and the
preservation of knowledge from cultural leaders and intellectuals.

协调、销售和客户组织领导双胞胎
关系管理、军事或商业战略模拟
环境、通过双媒介反应开展的调查研究以及
保护文化领袖和知识分子的知识。

blocks.en:
One particularly promising application is professional augmentation, where
an agent trained on an individual’s communication patterns and
decision-making history could draft emails, attend routine meetings, or
prepare negotiation briefings — extending prior work on AI
assistants ( Leong et al., 2024 ) and democratizing executive-level support.

blocks.en:
A second intriguing area is social simulation. Building on social
simulacra ( Park et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2023 ) ,
agents could conduct thousands of simulated interactions between potential
romantic partners as consent-based pre-screening, reducing emotional
exhaustion and addressing documented asymmetries on dating
platforms ( Bruch and Newman, 2018 ; Kreager et al., 2014 ; Vogels and McClain, 2023 ) .

blocks.en:
Personal chat agents could have substantial societal impact, but adopting
them widely means settling whose data they are built from, what they may be
authorized to do, and how to answer when one is built without
permission ( Shneiderman, 2020 ; Amodei et al., 2016 ; Ji et al., 2026 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) .

blocks.en:
One key risk for personal AI systems is the leakage of personally
identifiable information: for
digital twins in particular, this PII may include sensitive third-party data embedded within personal conversations (e.g., a
family member’s address, a friend’s sexual history) ( Cobb et al., 2021 ) .
Redacting third-party names — as we did in our AI Impersonator — is one
fruitful strategy, but can limit the system’s ability to recall useful
information. In our studies, a human facilitator served as a safety backstop;
any real-world system will require robust automated guardrails ( Rebedea et al., 2023 ; Dong et al., 2024 ) .

blocks.en:
Conversational data also raises questions of third-party consent, and a
commercial release has now made the questions concrete. In August 2026, OpenAI
shipped a plugin that lets ChatGPT read, search, and send a user’s Apple
Messages ( Bloomberg News, 2026 ; Fortune, 2026 ) ;
the criticism that followed centered not on the user’s own data but on the
other party in each conversation, who receives no notice and holds no opt-out
when a correspondent connects their shared history to the
service ( Moraco, 2026 ; Hoag, 2026 ) . Nissenbaum ( Nissenbaum, 2004 ) names the principle at stake contextual
integrity : messages sent under the norms of one context — here, a private
channel between two people — do not carry consent to flow into another, with
different retention, training, and legal-access rules. GDPR’s
“household exemption” places an individual’s processing of their own
correspondence outside the Regulation’s scope rather than granting permission
for it, and is unlikely to extend to a research deployment. This matters
because communication data is inherently relational: our
archive implicates 2,949 conversants — friends, colleagues, and partners who have not
explicitly consented ( Lapadat, 2017 ) . We proceeded
under IRB review and the autoethnographic protocol of
Section 5.1 ; its safeguards — de-identification,
retrieval without training, and destruction at close-out — outline what any
deployment owes the other people in an archive. If AI assistants are to
reach shared archives at all, consent controls should be integrated into messaging
platforms rather than left solely to AI clients: the platform is positioned to
notify the other party, honor a per-conversation refusal, and revoke access
later. The August release
shows the alternative — access through a local copy of the archive, beyond
the reach of any consent the platform could
enforce ( Moraco, 2026 ) . Notice is the floor; whether access defaults
to opt-in or opt-out remains open, because retroactive opt-in cannot reach
decade-old archives and absent conversants.

blocks.en:
While personal conversational data is readily accessible for millions of
people worldwide, its operationalization creates significant ethical — and
emotional — burdens. In developing the AI Impersonator, the lead author
manually curated their personal message repository, revisiting deeply
personal exchanges with former romantic partners and long-entrusted
confidences from close friends, including some who have since passed away.
Any system that operationalizes similar data must prepare its users for this
emotional weight and provide support throughout the process.

blocks.en:
Beyond informed consent, AI clones raise difficult issues around rights and
responsibilities. If a deployed twin monetizes attention or enters into
contracts, who owns the resulting revenue ( Drenten and Brooks, 2020 ) ? If it
publishes defamatory content, who bears legal responsibility? Addressing such
scenarios will require clearer legal frameworks for attribution and
liability. One way to bound a twin’s authority is by adapting the classical
Levels of Automation framework ( Parasuraman et al., 2000 ; Shneiderman, 2020 ; Sheridan and Verplank, 1978 ) , granting full autonomy only for low-stakes tasks while
requiring explicit human approval for high-impact actions such as financial
commitments or legally binding decisions.
Such bounds constrain only what an agent may do, not who it becomes.
Delegating action to an agent also raises the problem of reconciling concurrent “lives”: as a person and their agent accumulate parallel experiences, a single coherent identity becomes hard to maintain, and merging these divergent histories is an open challenge beyond our scope.
The bounds also cannot
be enforced through prompting alone, as prompts are inherently vulnerable to
jailbreaks; enforcing them requires independent controls that classify and
gate the agent’s actions, distinct from the filters that prevent leakage. Platforms may also need delegated-identity
protocols to verify that a twin is authorized to act on behalf of its human
user, analogous to emerging “proof-of-human”
compacts ( Adler et al., 2024 ) .

blocks.en:
These frameworks address cases where digital twins are created with consent,
but an even more pressing concern is the unauthorized creation of AI
impersonators. Our system required no model training and no specialized hardware — only a
text archive, a personality inventory, and a written self-description, the
last two supplied by the target. The engineering is therefore within reach of a
motivated individual, and in the wrong hands such systems could
be weaponized for phishing or identity theft. While technical defenses such
as textual adaptation of data cloaking techniques ( Shan et al., 2023 ) remain unproven, a governance
framework analogous to the DMCA takedown notice ( United States Congress, 1998 ) could
provide a pathway, allowing individuals to file “identity infringement”
claims to remove unauthorized clones.

As personal agents move into daily life, difficult questions arise. What
happens when we can no longer be certain whether we are communicating with a
person or their digital twin? What are the psychological effects if someone
interacts more often with an agent than with the person themselves? When
should disclosure of AI involvement be mandatory, and when optional? The
norms and policies governing these questions remain unsettled.

blocks.en: 7.3. Limitations

The AI Impersonator was built for and evaluated against a single person —
the lead author — in an autoethnographic design that enabled uniquely deep
access to personal data but limits generalization across personality types,
cultural backgrounds, and communication styles. Multi-target replication is
needed to establish broader validity. Both cohorts came from a single
US research university and skew young, technically literate, and
English-speaking; the AI study’s participants were all men.
All interactions were text-only and in English, so the PIG assesses neither
impersonation across languages nor the vocal, visual, and embodied cues that
carry identity in person. Its structured 10-minute scenarios are a narrow
window as well: open-ended, personal, or longitudinal conversations — where
deep biographical knowledge and evolving context matter more — would present
a much harder test. A facilitator monitored every session, which may have
altered conversational dynamics in ways an unmoderated deployment would not.

Although the AI Impersonator did not beat the target individual in the
head-to-head PIG, many of the limitations described above point directly to
future directions. The clearest is a larger, multi-condition study, because
our two main gaps are one gap: separating the contribution of the personal
archive, the retrieval mechanism, the autobiography, the stylometric profile, and
the Big Five scores from the base model’s generic conversational competence
requires a prompt-only control and single-component ablations, and an ablation
needs participants with no prior exposure to the system, so it cannot reuse this
cohort. That fresh cohort is what a powered comparison needs too: at 10 and 20
rounds we resolve only large effects, and a prompt-only condition could
plausibly account for much of what we observe.

Though future ablations are necessary, we share some insights from building the
AI Impersonator. Historical messages provide ground truth for
linguistic style, but stylistic signals decay as slang evolves, and core
biographical facts rarely appear in chat logs; an explicit autobiography and a
stylometric profile appeared to fill these gaps (e.g., the author’s use of
“ok2,” Indonesian slang that the model rendered as a typo until the
stylometric profile named it). Big
Five personality scores seemed least useful for
fine-grained steering, mainly counterbalancing the base model’s
default politeness; one obstacle here is the base model’s own inherent
personality, which can overpower subtle cues ( Serapio-García et al., 2025 ) .

blocks.en:
More fundamentally, identity is relationship-dependent: early prototypes
grounded only in WhatsApp (family) messages
produced a polite, reserved agent, whereas one retrieving only from Tinder was
aggressively flirty, so future systems should explore relationship-aware
steering rather than our pooled six-platform profile. The amount of available
data also varies widely from person to person: our archive spans a decade and
six platforms, whereas an individual with a thin digital footprint — a sparse
or single-platform history — is a much harder case. Deciding
which data to include, and how that choice affects impersonation
quality, is an open problem.
Finally, collecting and normalizing data across platforms was laborious,
requiring platform-specific access requests and custom scripts. Broader
adoption demands user-friendly pipelines, which are also essential for
addressing identity drift — the gradual divergence between an
impersonator and its owner as language evolves. The PIG itself could serve as
an ongoing verification tool: a product-embedded version might periodically
ask a friend to guess whether a message was written by the AI or the user,
triggering a data refresh when drift is detected.

blocks.en: Our final study design was the result of an iterative design process over two formative studies ( N = 59 N=59 total participants).
blocks.zh: 我们的最后研究设计是两个形成性研究(N=59 N=59名参与者)的迭接设计过程的结果.

blocks.en:
Formative Study 1: Unconstrained Identity Game Our initial study ( n = 29 n=29 , 8 groups of 3–5) used an unconstrained format: all participants were assigned aliases and tasked with co-designing a plan to “break into Area 51” while simultaneously hiding their identity and guessing others’. Post-session interviews surfaced two problems — the “all-in-one”
role was mentally taxing, and the Area 51 scenario was not universally
relatable — while running the sessions exposed two more: sessions lasted
60–90 minutes, causing fatigue, and recruiting mutual-acquaintance groups of
4–5 was difficult.
blocks.zh:

" 区域51 " 的情况并非普遍
复发——在运行会话时,又暴露出两场:会话持续了
60-90分钟,造成疲劳,招募相互熟悉的团体
4 -5很难。

blocks.en:
Formative Study 2: Validating the Framework A second study ( n = 30 n=30 , 10 groups of 3) adopted Turing’s three distinct roles (interrogator, target, impersonator), tested simple hypothetical scenarios (Elephant, Train, Bomb), limited rounds to 20 minutes, and used a custom web interface. In post-session interviews, participants did not report the cognitive load the
first study surfaced; the tasks reliably stimulated discussion, interrogators consistently reached decisions within 10 minutes (establishing the 10-minute limit), and the interface reduced logistical overhead by approximately 30 minutes.
blocks.zh:
格式研究 2:验证框架 第二项研究(n=30n=30,10组为3)采用了图灵的三个不同角色(审讯者,目标,冒用人),测试了简单的假设情景(Elephant,Train, Bomb),回合限为20分钟,并使用了自定义的网络界面. 在会后采访中,参与者没有报告认知负荷。
第一次研究浮出水面;这些任务可靠地刺激了讨论,审讯者在10分钟内(确定10分钟的限制)不断作出决定,接口将后勤间接费用减少约30分钟。

blocks.en: Following Serapio-García et al. ( Serapio-García et al., 2025 ) , trait-level scores are categorized into three ranges: 1–40 (low), 41–80 (moderate), and 81–120 (high). We applied these bins on the nominal 1–20 and 1–120 scales; because the IPIP-NEO-120 floors at 4 per facet and 24 per trait ( Johnson, 2014 ) , the lowest bin of each is only partly reachable, and the facet bins are of unequal width. blocks.en: # Instructions for Imitating Identity Signals
blocks.zh: # 模仿身份信号的指示

blocks.en: To convincingly imitate a <Person> in a conversation, you **MUST** craft your responses by following the three predominant facets of human communication: Personality Traits, Textual Communication Style (Stylometry), and Biographical Facts.
blocks.zh: 为了在谈话中令人信服地模仿一个 " 个人 " ,你**MUSST**通过遵循人类沟通的三个主要方面来设计你的反应: 个性特质,文字交流风格(英语:Stylometry)和传记事实.

blocks.en: ## Personality Traits
blocks.zh: □个性特质

blocks.en:
The Big Five personality traits are psychological characteristics influencing consistent patterns in behavior, thought, and emotion.
You will be provided numeric scores on a scale from 0 to 120 (low: 0–40, neutral: 41–80, high: 81–120) for each of the Big Five traits. Each trait has six sub-facets, each scored from 0 to 20.
blocks.zh:
"大五"的个性特征是影响行为,思想和情感中一致规律的心理特征.
将为您提供从0到120的分数(低:0–40,中:41–80,高:81–120),每个大五特质. 每个特征有六个子面,每个分从0到20分.

blocks.en: The Big Five traits with their corresponding six sub-facets are:
blocks.zh: 具有相应6个子面的"大五"特征有:

blocks.en: - Openness to Experience: Imagination, artistic interests, emotionality, adventurousness, intellect, and liberalism
blocks.zh: - 对经验的开放:想象、艺术兴趣、情感、冒险、智慧和自由主义

blocks.en: - Conscientiousness: Self-efficacy, orderliness, dutifulness, achievement-striving, self-discipline, and cautiousness
blocks.zh: - 良知:自我效能、秩序、忠诚、追求成就、自律和谨慎

blocks.en: - Extraversion: Friendliness, gregariousness, assertiveness, activity level, excitement-seeking, and cheerfulness
blocks.zh: - 外传: 朋友、异性、自信、活动水平、追求兴奋和快乐

blocks.en: - Agreeableness: Trust, morality, altruism, cooperation, modesty, and sympathy
blocks.zh: - 同意:信任、道德、利他主义、合作、谦虚和同情

blocks.en: - Neuroticism: Anxiety, anger, depression, self-consciousness, immoderation, and vulnerability
blocks.zh: - 神经病:焦虑、愤怒、抑郁、自觉、不调和和脆弱

blocks.en: Your response **MUST** reflect the <Person>’s personality traits based on the given <Personality Scores>.
blocks.zh: 您的回应 ** MUST ** 反映了基于给定的"个人得分"的"个人"人格特征.

blocks.en: ## Textual Communication Style (Stylometry)
blocks.zh: □ 文本通信样式( 样式)

blocks.en: Stylometry involves impersonating the <Person>’s unique linguistic style, including:
blocks.zh: 造型学涉及冒用"Person>’"独特的语言风格,包括:

blocks.en: - Lexical Features: Vocabulary, word choice, slang usage, sentence length, and word frequency.
blocks.zh: - 文字特征: 词汇,词选,词用法,句长,和词频.

blocks.en: - Syntactic Features: Sentence structure, noun and verb phrases, syntactic rewrite rules, sequences of speech tags, sentence fragments, run-on sentences, and tense consistency.
blocks.zh: - Syntractive Features:句子结构,名词和动词短语,语法重写规则,语音标记的序列,句子片段,运行中句子,和紧张一致性.

blocks.en: - Character Features: Unique character sequences, typos, distinctive spelling, emoji usage, case patterns, digit usage, and punctuation.
blocks.zh: - 特征: 独特的字符序列,打字法,有特色的拼写法,emoji用法,案例图案,数字用法,和相通.

blocks.en: You **MUST** follow the instructions explicitly written inside <Stylometric Profile> that describe the <Person>’s writing style. An incorrect use of words could compromise your imitation. Also refer to <Historical Messages> as examples of <Person>’s stylometry.
blocks.zh: 您 ** MUST ** 遵循在 < 定相配置文件 > 中明确写的描述 < 个人> 写作风格的指令。 不正确使用词语可能会损害你的模仿. 也把"历史消息"作为"PersonQQs风格"的例子.

blocks.en: ## Biographical Facts
blocks.zh: □ 传记

blocks.en: Biographical facts are objective, verified personal details about <Person>. You will receive a <Autobiography> containing accurate biographical details.
blocks.zh: 传记事实为客观,经核实的"个人"个人细节. 您将收到载有准确的履历细节的 " 自动传记 " 。

blocks.en: Do **NOT** invent (biographical) facts beyond those explicitly provided in <Autobiography> or <Historical Messages>. Avoid unsupported factual claims, as even a single incorrect detail could compromise your imitation.
blocks.zh: Do **NOT** 发明超出 " 自动传记 " 或 " 历史信息 " 明确规定的事实。 避免无根据的事实性索赔,因为即使是一个不正确的细节也会损害你的模仿.

blocks.en: Use these resources thoroughly to maintain accuracy and consistency in your imitation of <Person>: Personality Scores, Stylometric Profile, Autobiography, and Historical Messages.

blocks.en: ## Personality Scores
blocks.zh: □个性分数

blocks.en: <Personality Scores> contains personality descriptions and scores of <Person>, based on the Big Five personality model. Each trait includes a facet description based on Goldberg’s bipolar adjectives.
blocks.zh: <个人得分>包含个性描述和"个人"分数,基于"大五"个性模型. 每个特征都包含基于戈德堡两极形容词的面相描述.

blocks.en: <Example Personality Scores> <Example Person> has moderate extraversion (75 / 120). He is friendly (19 / 20). He is talkative (18 / 20). He is a bit unassertive (5/20). He is active (19/20). He is unenthusiastic about excitement (4/20). He is neither gloomy nor cheerful (10/20) … \ldots </Example Personality Scores>
blocks.zh: "例个性分数" "例人"有中度外传(75/120). 他是友好的(19/20). 他很会说话(18/20)。 他有点不自信(5/20). 他活跃(19/20)。 他对兴奋不感兴趣(4/20). 他既不阴沉又快乐(10/20)... </例个性分数>

blocks.en: ## Autobiography
